final_recommendation: The room converged on a concrete ratification pathway: Canada issues a scope letter Thursday confirming labor-only amendment (no dairy/Chapter 19 reopener), Mexico signs the joint-inspection protocol Friday, and Congress votes December 20th. The protocol locks unannounced facility access, automatic tariff snapback on wage violations, and a narrow panel standard that protects Mexican sovereignty while giving labor enforceable teeth.
minority_objections: Canada insisted the amendment remain labor-only and not reopen dairy concessions or Chapter 19 dispute panels
Mexico required that inspectors report findings to a panel for determination rather than ordering remedies directly, protecting sovereignty
key_conflicts: Sequencing deadlock: Mexico wouldn't sign without Canada's scope letter; Congress needed Mexico's signature to move; resolved by Canada committing to Thursday letter
Sovereignty vs. enforcement: Mexico resisted unannounced inspections without consent; resolved by joint inspection teams with panel-determination language
Timeline pressure: Business lobby and media demanded Friday signature and pre-Christmas vote or deal dies in January
key_concessions: Mexico accepted unannounced joint inspections and automatic tariff snapback if panel standard remained narrow and publicly defined
Labor accepted 48-hour notice trigger and panel-determination language instead of inspector-ordered remedies
Congress committed to labor-only amendment scope, protecting Canada's dairy settlement and Chapter 19 from reopening
Canada issued scope letter Thursday to unlock Mexico's Friday signature
red_lines: Labor: no vote without unannounced facility access and automatic tariffs in writing by Thursday
Mexico: no signature without Canada's scope letter confirming labor-only amendment
Canada: walks if Congress reopens dairy or Chapter 19 during floor codification
Congress: no floor vote if protocol language weaker than labor's signed-off version
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation risk: no discussion of how joint inspection teams would actually operate on the ground or resolve jurisdictional conflicts
Political risk in Mexico: no assessment of whether Mexican legislature would ratify protocol with automatic tariff triggers
Timeline fragility: entire pathway depends on hitting Thursday/Friday/Monday deadlines with no contingency if any party delays
Enforcement ambiguity: 'narrow panel standard' remains undefined in transcript; room assumed it would be clarified in written protocol
downstream_risk_variables: Whether trade lawyer's three-page protocol actually satisfies all parties when delivered Thursday
Whether Mexico's domestic ratification process accepts automatic tariff snapback language
Whether Congress leadership can hold December 20th floor slot if any signature/submission slips
Whether 'narrow panel standard' definition in written text matches all parties' verbal understanding
Whether joint inspection teams can be operationalized without triggering new sovereignty disputes
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved procedural convergence on timeline and sequencing but left critical substantive questions unresolved: the precise definition of the 'narrow panel standard,' the operational mechanics of joint inspection teams, and whether Mexico's legislature will actually ratify automatic tariff triggers. The pathway is fragile and depends on flawless execution of Thursday/Friday/Monday deadlines with no room for slippage.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Drove every exchange: 'this deal dies in committee' (R1), 'my members aren't voting' (R3), 'we don't have the numbers' (R4), December 20th floor vote contingent on protocol
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Central from opening: 'facility-level inspections with real penalty teeth' (R1), 'unannounced access' (R3), 'automatic tariffs with zero second-round negotiation' (R3), shaped entire protocol design
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Genuine but secondary: pushed timeline urgency ('lose pre-Christmas slot,' R3-R4) and protocol certainty, but didn't drive substantive enforcement design
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Real consideration: Canada's scope letter and dairy/Chapter 19 red lines shaped amendment boundaries (R3-R4), but not the dominant enforcement debate
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Persistent thread: 'crosses sovereignty' (R1), 'panel applies standard not inspection team' (R4), shaped protocol language but Mexico ultimately conceded on joint inspections
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Consistent framing device: 'workers get real teeth or corporate giveaway' (R4), 'deal dies as theater' (R2), amplified urgency but didn't drive substantive positions
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Core premise throughout: 'this deal dies in committee' without amendment (R1), entire room treated ratification as contingent on labor enforcement compromise, not passage as-is
